name: Adam Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. What happens on a normal day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and manage ten people who schedule repair crews across a large company’s sites. I read the overnight faults, assign the urgent jobs and call a site when a crew cannot make the promised time. I use AI every day to group work orders and spot two jobs on the same route, but I check with the crew lead before moving anything. I like getting a broken lift fixed before someone is stranded; I dislike the spreadsheet meetings that hide who is waiting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where do you stand at work, and what is at stake at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I have a bachelor’s degree and have managed this team for seven years; I’m about average among the company’s managers. My partner, Jo, is an occupational therapist, and our children are eight and fifteen. The mortgage takes both incomes, and we have about four months of expenses saved; my pay is typical and there are some similar offices nearby. I’m active in our staff union because the people who answer the faults should see the staffing plan before it is decided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a quicker route list is useful, but a crew lead should confirm what can fit in the van. I would keep the person waiting for a repair in the picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My role should continue, and four months saved makes an ordinary delay manageable. I still dislike how quickly the company turns a small time saving into a new target for the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep the morning crew call and use AI only to group work orders before the lead checks the route. In the first year Jo and I would keep sending 130 monthly to savings while both wages hold, and I’d ask the union representative to review any new response target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our income. The union question is about fair targets, not a fear that my job ends tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which fault gets moved first on a busy morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A broken lift at the care site gets the first available crew. A smarter route list is useless if the person in a wheelchair cannot reach the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask the union about a small target change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crew should see how a new number is set. Saving ten minutes on a route does not mean every repair takes ten minutes less.

say: I’d keep **crew leads** checking every proposed repair route before dispatch.
A person waiting for a **repair** should still guide our daily priorities.
think: My **management role** continues in a plateau.
Four months saved protect us, though **new targets** still bother me.
do: Keep the **morning crew call** and verify AI routes with a lead.
Save **130 monthly** while both wages hold and ask the union to review targets.
feel: I feel **calm** about income and alert to targets.
S0.quote: A smarter route list is useless if the person in a wheelchair cannot reach the floor.
fieldNote: He uses **AI daily** but confirms routes with a crew lead.
Four months saved buffer an **ordinary delay**.
His union concern is **target setting**, not imminent job loss.

steps.text: Keep morning repair-crew calls and verify AI route groups with the crew lead
Transfer 130 monthly to savings while both household wages hold
Ask the union representative to review any new repair-response target

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crews that scheduling and customer replies are the first jobs software will take. I’d publish the missed-visit count beside any claim that the tool saves staff time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten schedulers could become five, and then my manager post may be combined with another team. I’m good at using the system, but being good at shrinking a queue could still shrink my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I’d run an AI scheduling trial on sixty closed repair jobs and ask crew leads to mark each impossible route. In the first year I’d complete the company’s paid audit training and bring the trial results to the union before management sets new staffing levels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about losing my own post and about the people who answer the angry calls. Having evidence gives me some control, but not the final decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the schedulers before the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the trial could change posts and show them the sixty jobs we are using. They should be able to point out an impossible route before a manager signs off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you publish a result that supports fewer staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, with the missed visits and the proposed cuts on the same page. I will not separate the useful tool from the people it displaces.

say: I’d show **missed visits** beside claimed time savings.
Staff should see **proposed scheduling cuts** beside trial results before management settles new team sizes.
think: A merged scheduling team could remove **my manager post**, even after seven years leading this crew.
My daily tool skill does not guarantee **continued pay** if the company needs fewer managers.
do: Trial AI on **sixty old jobs** with crew leads marking impossible routes.
Complete **paid audit training** and bring staffing evidence to the union.
feel: I feel **anxious** about our posts but able to test.
S1.quote: I will not separate the useful tool from the people it displaces.
fieldNote: He refuses to hide **staffing effects** behind efficiency figures.
His own post is exposed despite **daily AI use**.
Paid training teaches him to **audit the tool**, not merely accept it.

steps.text: Test AI schedules against sixty closed repair jobs with crew lead review
Complete the company-paid scheduling audit training
Bring trial and staffing figures to the union before cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company for dates, severance terms and a named contact for sites whose repairs are mishandled. I’d ask the union to put those questions to management together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could plan, schedule and answer better than I can, so I expect my role to go. Jo’s hands-on therapy may last until robots arrive around 2031, but her wage alone would not pay the mortgage and our children’s costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week Jo and I would pause the planned bathroom renovation and keep its deposit in cash. Before 2028 I’d help the union seek paid transition time and meet our mortgage lender to ask what a job-loss payment plan would require; in the first year after AGI, I’d apply for a posted on-site repair coordinator role only if its written pay covers my mortgage share and includes real site visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed. Four months saved is helpful, but I would wake up worrying about both the 2028 desk cut and the later risk to Jo’s work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the on-site role really be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The site visit itself may need a person until about 2031, but its scheduling and reports face AGI in 2028 too. A site coordinator title is no shelter from 2028 AGI when its reports and schedules can be automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the lender cannot offer relief?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would use the cash we kept from the renovation and keep making the mortgage payment while searching. I would not count a payment pause until it was written down.

say: Sites need a **named repair contact** after automation.
The union should take **staff questions** to management together.
think: Jo’s therapy may last until **2031 robots**, but one wage cannot cover us.
do: Pause the **bathroom renovation** and keep its deposit available.
Seek **union transition time** and apply for posted site work only with pay covering my mortgage share and real visits.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by two household deadlines.
S2.quote: A site coordinator title is no shelter from 2028 AGI when its reports and schedules can be automated.
fieldNote: He sees **2028 AGI** in both his desk and a site coordinator’s reports.
Jo’s therapy provides a **temporary second wage** before 2031 robots.
Lender relief is an **inquiry**, never counted as granted.

steps.text: Pause the bathroom renovation and retain its deposit for mortgage payments
Help the union ask for paid transition time before 2028
Apply for posted site coordination after 2028 only with mortgage-share pay and real visits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives management time to publish job numbers and negotiate paid changes with the union. I would want the repair sites to see how missed visits are counted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could stay on salary while our older child finishes school and build a larger reserve before 2031. A site coordinator still writes plans and reports, so AGI would reach that work in 2031; physical repair follows robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January 2027 I’d raise our monthly savings transfer to 200 only while both wages hold and the mortgage is current. I’d ask the union to negotiate paid redeployment periods and apply for an advertised site operations role before 2031 only if its wage covers my mortgage share and it includes hands-on visits; after AGI arrives, I’d stay only while those visits remain paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but five years gives us more paychecks to prepare. I would rather negotiate time and a written wage than collect certificates I cannot use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if management offers a course without a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask which posted role and wage follows it. I will not use family evenings for a badge with no opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave before the 2031 date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a written site offer that keeps the mortgage paid. I would keep the current income until that exists.

say: I’d seek **job numbers** and paid redeployment terms.
Workers need **written pay** before moving into another role.
think: More paychecks could build a **larger reserve** before my scheduling post changes.
Site plans and reports still face **2031 AGI** before physical repair robots arrive in 2034.
do: Save **200 monthly** only while wages hold and the mortgage is current.
Negotiate **paid redeployment** and take site work only with a written viable wage.
Stay in **site operations** after 2031 only while paid human visits remain.
feel: I feel **anxious** but have time to bargain.
S3.quote: I will not use family evenings for a badge with no opening.
fieldNote: He rejects **unattached certificates** when no posted job or wage follows the course.
His site alternative retains **2031 thinking exposure**.
The savings increase requires **both wages** and a current mortgage.

steps.text: Transfer 200 monthly to savings only while both wages hold and mortgage is current
Ask the union to negotiate paid redeployment periods
Apply for advertised site operations only if wages cover mortgage share and visits are hands-on

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade lets the company put a real schedule and training money in front of workers. We should not wait until the last repair planner is called into a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036, with both children older and perhaps out of school. If Jo and I keep earning, we could pay down the mortgage and build a longer reserve. A site coordinator’s planning still faces 2036 AGI and the physical repairs face robots around 2039, so I would not claim permanent safety there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January 2027 Jo and I would add 150 monthly to mortgage principal only while our four-month reserve stays intact. I’d keep documenting missed repairs for the union, seek a written paid redeployment agreement before 2036 and apply for a posted site role only if its wage covers our mortgage share; after AGI arrives, I’d keep that role only while paid human site work exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy but able to organize. Ten years would let us protect the house without pretending a title is a lifetime shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union to put in the agreement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A notice date, paid time to learn another job and the wage for each opening. A general promise to be fair does not buy a week of groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a site role with only reports?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The reports are thinking work exposed in 2036; I would need real visits and written pay before moving.

say: I’d ask for a **real change schedule** and training money.
Workers need **notice** before the last planner is cut.
think: I could reduce the **mortgage** if both wages hold.
Site reports face **2036 AGI** before 2039 repair robots.
do: Add **150 monthly** to mortgage principal only while four months saved remain intact.
Seek **paid redeployment terms** and posted site work only with pay covering my mortgage share and real visits.
Keep the **site role** after 2036 only while paid human work exists.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but able to organize.
S4.quote: A general promise to be fair does not buy a week of groceries.
fieldNote: He ties **union terms** to notice, paid time and listed wages.
He protects a **four-month reserve** before mortgage overpayments.
He still sees **thinking exposure** in an on-site title.

steps.text: Pay 150 extra monthly toward the mortgage only while four months of savings remain
Ask the union for written notice dates paid learning time and wages by opening
Apply for posted site work before 2036 only with mortgage-share pay and real visits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our mortgage needs two wages and my scheduling post could end before we have a new plan. Written severance, a paid redeployment period and posted jobs with wages would help. Jo’s work buys time, not immunity from the later robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who tells the person waiting for a lift repair that a route looked efficient on a screen. A missed repair is still a person stuck on the wrong floor.

headlineQuote: A missed repair is still a person stuck on the wrong floor.
portrait: **Adam**, 43, is an experienced repair-scheduling manager with a bachelor’s degree.
Typical pay and **four months saved** support a mortgage and two children.
He uses **AI daily** and takes test results to the union alongside staffing effects.
He seeks **paid redeployment** without treating another planning title as shelter.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his scheduling role while Jo’s therapy remains a temporary second wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid redeployment and posted jobs with wages would let the family plan.
